::: {.callout-tip}
#### Learning Objectives

- Know how to log2 transform DIA precursor data within a `QFeatures` object
- Understand how to use `robustSummary` to summarise precursor-level data to protein-level abundance, including in the presence of missing values
- Understand the importance of visualising missing values at the protein level
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| purl: false

knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = here::here("course_files/dia"))
```

```{r}
#| label: load-packages-and-data
#| include: false

library("QFeatures")
library("tidyr")
library("dplyr")
library("ggplot2")

load("preprocessed/lesson03.rda", verbose = TRUE)
```

Having filtered our DIA-NN data to retain only high-confidence identifications and removed precursors with excessive missing values, we are now ready to continue processing.
The precursor quantities were normalised by DIA-NN before we imported them.
In this lesson we will log2 transform the precursor-level data and aggregate to protein-level abundances ready for downstream statistical analysis.

## Logarithmic transformation

If we look at the distribution of untransformed precursor intensities, we will see that the abundance values are dramatically skewed towards zero.

```{r}
#| label: histogram-untransformed-abundance
#| warning: false
#| message: false

dia_qf[["precursors_filtered_missing"]] %>%
  assay() %>%
  longForm() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_bw() +
  xlab("Abundance (untransformed)")
```

{{< include ../_shared/_log_transformation.md >}}

::: {.callout-note}
#### At which stage should log transformation be applied?

Logarithmic transformation should be applied at the appropriate stage of the processing pipeline for the aggregation method being used.
Here we apply it **before** aggregation to protein level, because we use `robustSummary` for summarisation.
`robustSummary` fits a linear model to the precursor-level data, which assumes approximately Gaussian distributed residuals --- a requirement that is only met after log transformation.
:::

We apply a log2 transformation to the filtered precursor data using the `logTransform` function, which creates a new set in our `QFeatures` object.

```{r}
#| label: log-transform
dia_qf <- logTransform(
  dia_qf,
  base = 2,
  i = "precursors_filtered_missing",
  name = "precursors_filtered_missing_log"
)
```

## Summarising to protein-level abundance

We now aggregate from precursor level to protein level using the `aggregateFeatures` function.
For DIA data with missing values, we use the `robustSummary` method (@Sticker2020), which models the log-transformed peptide/precursor-level quantification as being dependent upon the protein-level abundance plus a precursor-level effect.
This modelling-based approach can handle missing values without imputation, as it only considers finite data.

We aggregate on the `Protein.Group` column, which holds the protein group DIA-NN inferred for each precursor.
`Protein.Ids` lists every protein a precursor matches before inference, so aggregating on it would split one inferred group across several features that carry the same `Genes` and `Protein.Names` annotation, since those columns describe the protein group.

`robustSummary` fits its model with `MASS::rlm`, and extra arguments given to `aggregateFeatures` are passed on to it.
We set `maxit = 10000` to raise the iteration limit of `rlm` from its default of 20, so that the fit can converge rather than stopping early.

```{r}
#| label: qfeatures-aggregate-precursors-to-proteins
#| message: false

dia_qf <- aggregateFeatures(
  dia_qf,
  i = "precursors_filtered_missing_log",
  fcol = "Protein.Group",
  name = "proteins",
  fun = MsCoreUtils::robustSummary,
  maxit = 10000
)

dia_qf
```

{{< include ../_shared/_two_peptide_rule.md >}}

::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Quantification completeness at the protein level

{{< level 2 >}}

Although `robustSummary` can handle missing values at the precursor level, a protein will still have a missing abundance in any sample where all of its precursors are absent.

To investigate this, we will use the `longForm` function, which converts a `QFeatures` set from wide format (proteins × samples) to long format (one row per protein--sample combination).
The `colvars` argument specifies which columns from the `colData` to carry across.

Run the following code and inspect the output --- what does each row represent?

```{r}
#| label: show-protein-long-form
# dia_qf[,,'proteins'] subsets the QFeatures object to the "proteins" set
longForm(dia_qf[,, 'proteins'], colvars = 'group') %>%
  data.frame() %>%
  head()
```

Now use this long-format data to create a plot showing how many samples each protein is quantified in, broken down by group.
Then consider:

- Why might some proteins still be missing in some samples despite using `robustSummary`?
- What happens to proteins quantified in only a few samples of a group in the rest of our workflow?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>Count the number of finite values per protein
per group using `sum(is.finite(value))`.</details>

::::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}
Each row in the long-format data represents one protein--sample observation, with `value` containing the protein abundance and `group` indicating which experimental group that sample belongs to.

```{r}
#| label: histogram-quantified-samples-per-group
longForm(dia_qf[,, 'proteins'], colvars = 'group') %>%
  data.frame() %>%
  group_by(rowname, group) %>%
  summarise(n_quant = sum(is.finite(value))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n_quant)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  facet_wrap(~group) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = 'Quantified samples', y = 'Proteins')
```

`robustSummary` estimates protein abundance from whatever precursors are observed in a given sample.
If *no* precursors for a protein are observed in that sample, there is no data from which to estimate abundance, so the protein-level value remains missing regardless of the summarisation method.

Proteins quantified in fewer than three samples of any group are removed before testing in the statistical analysis lesson, as described in the previous lesson.
:::::
:::

```{r}
#| label: save-lesson04
#| include: false

save(dia_qf, file = "preprocessed/lesson04.rda")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key Points

- Log2 transformation is applied to precursor-level data before aggregation to protein level, giving data a more Gaussian distribution suitable for downstream statistical analysis
- `robustSummary` is the recommended summarisation method for DIA data, as it can handle missing values at the precursor level without requiring imputation
- Proteins where all precursors are missing in a given sample will still have missing protein-level abundances, even with `robustSummary`
:::
